content: Ammonium bituminosulfonate, also known as ichthyol or ichthammol (CAS 8029-68-3), is a naturally derived substance obtained through the dry distillation of sulfur-rich oil shale. It is widely used in medicine for the treatment of various skin conditions, including acne, eczema, and psoriasis. Typically, it is formulated as an ointment in concentrations of 10% or 20%, often referred to as a drawing salve or black ointment. The dermatological properties of ammonium bituminosulfonate were first identified by the Austrian physician Paul Gerson Unna. Based on elemental analysis, its chemical composition is approximated as C28H36S5O6(NH4)2. However, as a natural product, it is a complex mixture of numerous compounds. Chemically, it is classified as a sulfonated shale oil and exists in two forms: pale sulfonated shale oil (PSSO) and dark sulfonated shale oil (DSSO). DSSO is sometimes specifically referred to as ichthammol. This form is a thick, reddish-brown liquid with a characteristic bituminous odor and taste. It is water-soluble and miscible with glycerin but is nearly insoluble in strong alcohol or concentrated ether. It contains a high percentage of organically bound sulfur. Ichthyol is chemically incompatible with acids, alkali carbonates or hydrates, and alkaloidal salts. Pharmacologically, both PSSO and DSSO exhibit anti-inflammatory, bactericidal, and fungicidal properties. In otology, a mixture of glycerol and ichthammol (commonly referred to as G & I) has been used for generations as a topical treatment for ear infections. It is particularly effective against Gram-positive organisms. The anti-inflammatory effects of ichthyol are attributed to its modulation of the formation, secretion, and activity of inflammatory mediators. DSSO is well-tolerated, and no evidence of teratogenic, mutagenic, or carcinogenic effects has been observed. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has published a Summary Report on ichthyol substances (also known as bituminosulfonates) as part of the European Maximum Residue Limits (MRL) procedure in veterinary medicine. In June 2005, the Committee for Medicinal Products for Veterinary Use (CVMP) concluded that due to its excellent tolerance and safety profile, there is no need to establish an MRL for ichthyol substances. Consequently, ichthyol can be applied topically to all mammalian food-producing species without restriction.
